title: Agent Evals, Looped Transformers, and Sub-3-Bit Quants
intro: Today's update highlights structural shifts in model architectures, quantization techniques, and evaluation practices. From looped transformers and 10 GB agent-capable models to harness sensitivity in agent benchmarks, here is what changed.

stories.headline: Z.ai debuts GLM-5.4 with a looped transformer architecture
stories.summary: Z.ai has released GLM-5.4, introducing a looped transformer architecture that executes weight-shared layers iteratively during forward passes to deepen the network without increasing parameter count. The model follows a design pattern seen in Inkling 2 Mini, which runs middle layers three times per token to improve reasoning efficiency on agentic tasks. GLM-5.4 is accessible via Z.ai's OpenAI-compatible API endpoint using their Coding Plan subscription key.
stories.why_it_matters: Looped architectures provide a parameter-efficient approach to boosting reasoning depth for agentic coding workloads.
stories.reason: Z.ai released GLM-5.4 featuring a looped transformer architecture that executes layers iteratively during forward passes to improve generalized coding performance.

item.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
item.summary:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

item.content:
23rd November 2026 - Link Blog
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer. GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:
In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.
This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:
Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.
GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.
It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.
I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.
Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:
I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.
It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.
I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

stories.headline: NariQ compresses Qwen3.8-27B into sub-3-bit GGUFs while preserving BF16 performance
stories.summary: Nari-labs released NariQ v1, compressing Qwen3.8-27B down to sub-3-bit GGUF files that fit within a 10 GB footprint. The method uses trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on real coding-agent execution traces. Benchmarks on long-horizon agentic tasks show the 3-bit and 2.5-bit variants match full BF16 performance on DeepSWE and math evaluations when served via a modified llama.cpp fork.
stories.why_it_matters: Sub-3-bit quantization calibrated on agent traces enables high-precision agentic reasoning on consumer GPUs within a 10 GB memory budget.
stories.reason: NariQ introduces sub-3-bit quantization methods for Qwen3.8-27B that compress the model into 10 GB while preserving near-BF16 accuracy on long-horizon agentic benchmarks.

item.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
item.summary:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.
To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.
Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):
- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4
- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0
- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6
- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9
Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below
(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):
- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7
- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8
- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8
Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork:
( https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp )
Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

stories.headline: Hugging Face details best practices and pitfalls in agentic evaluations
stories.summary: Hugging Face published a comprehensive guide on designing and maintaining evaluation suites for non-deterministic LLM agents. The guide highlights how execution environments skew results, pointing out an audit where changing the agent harness while holding the model fixed altered Terminal-Bench accuracy by up to 29.9 percentage points. To address these discrepancies, the authors break down the eight-step lifecycle of an agentic evaluation and offer guidelines for open-sourcing evaluation components.
stories.why_it_matters: Understanding harness-induced variance is essential for building robust benchmarks and isolating true model capability.
stories.reason: Hugging Face published a practical guide on designing and maintaining robust evaluation suites specifically engineered for non-deterministic AI agents.

item.title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
item.content:
How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
Overview
AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.
Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.
The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.
This guide covers four things:
- Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score.
- The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A.
- When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected.
- What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected.
In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.
1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed
AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.
Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.
Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.
We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.
The anatomy of an agentic evaluation
Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.
There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.
Why benchmark release decisions matter
Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.
At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts…

stories.headline: llama.cpp automates Pareto-optimized quantization selection
stories.summary: The latest llama.cpp release (b12669) adds an automated Pareto-optimization feature to target specific file sizes or bits-per-weight limits while minimizing quantization error. The system dynamically selects optimal tensor precision using weighted cosine error metrics and centered-normalized importance scaling. It also introduces state checkpointing and parallelized tensor processing to streamline long quantization jobs.
stories.why_it_matters: Automated tensor-level Pareto optimization allows inference engines to maximize model quality under strict VRAM caps without manual tuning.
stories.reason: llama.cpp added an automatic Pareto-optimization quantizer that dynamically selects optimal tensor precision to hit target file sizes or bits-per-weight at minimal error.

stories.headline: Duopra brings real-time tool execution to full-duplex speech models
stories.summary: Duopra introduces real-time tool invocation and argument revision into full-duplex conversational models without losing natural turn-taking capability. Evaluated on Full-Duplex-Bench v3, prior speech systems frequently failed before executing domain tools due to incomplete or misdirected requests. By combining protocol SFT, full-duplex RL, and projector-only repair, Duopra raised direct tool execution Pass@1 performance from 26.0% after SFT to 47.7%.
stories.why_it_matters: Full-duplex models can now handle mid-stream tool execution and argument corrections during continuous voice agent sessions.
stories.reason: Duopra investigates moving full-duplex models beyond spoken conversation into real-time tool invocation and dynamic argument revision mid-stream.

item.content:
Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency
Abstract
Full-duplex interaction models exhibit strong conversational agency, enabling natural, low-latency turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. However, completing tasks further requires task agency: timely tool invocation and argument revision following user corrections. Frontend-backend agents separate initiation from execution: the frontend decides whether and what to request, while the backend determines how. Execution can be offloaded, but unsent requests cannot be executed, and incomplete ones can misdirect the backend. On Full-Duplex-Bench v3 (FDB v3), most failures of Realtime-Venus-Audio + Harness in our streaming pipeline occur before a domain tool executes. We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex interaction model that learns task execution alongside conversational control. Duopra treats the backend as a tool, accepting a self-contained natural-language request. Direct calls and backend delegation share an action interface and requirements for faithful initiation and correct execution. Its three-stage training combines protocol SFT, full-duplex RL rewarding timely and complete execution, and projector-only repair of talker conditioning after thinker updates. With the same backend, Pass@1 rises from 4.7% to 44.7%; Duopra achieves 47.7% calling tools directly (26.0% after SFT) and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend. It improves three FDB v1.0 takeover rates over the base model. These results show that task agency can coexist with key conversational agency.
Community
We introduce Duopra, a full-duplex speech model that brings task agency into real-time conversational interaction. Duopra learns to invoke tools and delegate tasks while preserving natural turn-taking and interruption handling.
On Full-Duplex-Bench v3, Duopra achieves 47.7% Pass@1 with direct tool execution and 49.3% with a DeepSeek backend, demonstrating that conversational agency and task agency can coexist.
Project & Demo: https://cychen2003.github.io/duopra/

stories.headline: AgentRoboCritic provides action-level intent evaluation for direct robot control
stories.summary: The AgentRoboCritic framework shifts embodied agent evaluation from overall episode pass rates to step-by-step action critique. By requiring the policy agent to state local intent alongside each action, the evaluation revealed that 49.8% of successful episodes contained at least one failed action, with agents recovering in 57.7% of those failures. The team also released a fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic model, achieving 74.24% failure-mode classification accuracy at over 30 times lower cost than GPT-6 Astra.
stories.why_it_matters: Action-level intent feedback provides explicit diagnostic visibility into agent error recovery dynamics during step-by-step execution loops.
stories.reason: AgentRoboCritic provides a granular benchmark for frontier models driving low-level control, analyzing dynamic tool and step execution failures rather than just high-level task completion.

item.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
item.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. item.content:
AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
Abstract
Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.
Community
🤖 Can frontier agents control robots directly with low-level actions? And how do we actually tell how good they are?
📉 Existing evaluations focus on episode-level scores such as success rates. They hide the action-level feedback that is key to improving embodied agents!
💡 We introduce AgentRoboCritic. The policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates every action against it. For a failed action, the critic also returns its failure mode. With GPT-6 Astra as the critic, we annotate 12,844 actions across 12 manipulation benchmarks.
🔍 What the action-level feedback reveals:
- Closed-loop recovery: 49.8% of successful episodes contain at least one failed action, and 57.7% of failed actions are recovered by the end of the episode.
- Reliable semantic grounding: acting on the wrong object, order or category accounts for only 0.2% of failed actions.
- Strong zero-shot manipulation: GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 91% of RoboTwin 2.0 and 90% of YAMLab episodes, where π0.5 reaches 6% and 0%.
- The remaining bottleneck is physical execution: Grasp is the leading failure mode on most benchmarks.
🚀 To make action-level feedback low-cost, we release the 12,844 annotated actions, a 400-action human-annotated benchmark, and a fine-tuned Muse-Glimmer-30B critic. Its failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.6% to 74.2%, at over 30× lower cost than GPT-6 Astra.

stories.headline: Qwen 32B exhibits latent detection of prior concept injections
stories.summary: Researchers demonstrated that Qwen 32B internally detects when concepts have been injected into earlier context layers, even when its generated text denies any manipulation. Logit lens analysis showed clear detection signals within the residual stream that attenuate before final generation layers. Prompting the model with accurate information about introspection mechanisms increased injection detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
stories.why_it_matters: Latent residual stream monitoring can serve as an internal detection layer for prompt injection and hidden context manipulations.
stories.reason: Latent Introspection demonstrates that LLMs can internally detect prior concept injections in their activation space, with practical implications for interpretability and safety monitoring.

item.title: Latent Introspection: LLMs Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
item.content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Feb 2026 (v1), last revised 7 Nov 2026 (this version, v3)]
Title:Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

quick_hits.line: MemOnce proposes a scalable memory architecture designed to bypass standard token-level KV cache growth during long-horizon deployments.

item.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
item.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. headlines.headline: NariQ compresses Qwen3.8-27B into 10 GB with near-BF16 quality
headlines.blurb: NariQ uses 3-bit quantization to fit Qwen3.8-27B into 10 GB while maintaining BF16 performance across math and agentic tasks.

item.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
item.summary:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.
To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.
Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):
- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6
- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4
- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0
- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6
- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9
Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below
(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):
- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7
- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8
- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8
Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork:
( https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp )
Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.
